subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Obtain the reduction formula for I_n = ∫ secⁿx dx. Hence find ∫ sec⁵x dx.

mark_split.label: Apply by parts and use tan²x = sec²x − 1
Substitute n = 5, 3, 1 for the final answer

insider_note: Every term in this reduction and its final answer is positive — if a minus sign appears anywhere while working secⁿx, it has leaked in from the cscⁿx version worked alongside it, and is a sign something was copied from the wrong column.

steps.label: Set up integration by parts
lines: Given I_n = ∫ secⁿx dx = ∫ secⁿ⁻²x · sec²x dx
steps.why: Peeling off sec²x (whose antiderivative tanx is already known) leaves secⁿ⁻²x to differentiate — the same by-parts pattern as sinⁿx and cosⁿx, now with sec²x as the piece integrated.
common_mistakes: Peeling off only one secx instead of sec²x, which leaves an antiderivative that is not directly known.
Taking u = sec²x and v = secⁿ⁻²x the wrong way round.
steps.memory_tip: Always integrate the sec²x piece (v = tanx is a known standard result); differentiate the rest.

steps.label: Apply by parts and use tan²x = sec²x − 1
steps.why: tan²x = sec²x − 1 turns the new integral back into powers of secx alone, closing the loop back to I_n and I_{n−2} — the secant partner of the sin²x = 1 − cos²x step used for sinⁿx.
common_mistakes: Leaving tan²x un-replaced, which never returns to I_n or I_{n−2}.
Writing tan²x = 1 − sec²x with the sign reversed.
steps.memory_tip: tan²x = sec²x − 1, always positive on the sec²x side — the reverse of the cos²x identity's sign.

steps.label: Solve for the reduction formula
steps.why: Collecting the I_n terms on one side gives (n−1)I_n, not nI_n, because this by-parts split produced a −(n−2)I_n term rather than a −(n−1)I_n term — dividing by (n−1) is what makes this reduction's denominator different from the sinⁿx and cosⁿx ones.
common_mistakes: Dividing by n out of habit, copying the sinⁿx/cosⁿx pattern instead of the (n−1) that this derivation actually gives.
Losing the (n−2) coefficient on the second term.
steps.memory_tip: sinⁿx and cosⁿx divide by n; secⁿx and cscⁿx divide by (n−1) — a genuinely different denominator.

steps.label: Substitute n = 5, 3, 1 for the final answer
lines: and I₁ = ∫secx dx = log|secx + tanx| + c
So I₃ = secx tanx/2 + (1/2)log|secx + tanx| + c
steps.why: Odd n stops at I₁ = ∫secx dx, the standard log|secx + tanx| result — the same odd-n stopping rule as tanⁿx, but landing on a different standard integral.
common_mistakes: Stopping the chain at I₃ without substituting the value of I₁ into it.
Writing log|secx + tanx| as log|secx − tanx| by sign slip.
steps.memory_tip: secⁿx (odd n) stops at I₁ = log|secx+tanx|; cscⁿx (odd n) stops at I₁ = log|tan(x/2)| — different constants, same shape.
